prompt.context: Your client is a Consumer Packaged Goods company that produces frozen dough for uses in making bread loaves, pizza crusts, cookies, bagels, etc. This is a family-owned company with $2 billion in annual sales and two primary distribution channels: wholesale restaurant suppliers and supermarket chain bakeries. The dough is not branded, meaning there is no customer differentiation. Shelf life is 180 days, with customers requiring 60 days remaining upon receipt. Recipes are very similar across the industry with high recipe switching costs. The company has been experiencing a significantly higher spoilage rate than competitors. Competitors average about 2.5% spoilage; the client's rate last year was 10%. The client already reduced it to 7.5% by implementing a strict First-In-First-Out inventory management system at its warehouses and by donating inventory close to expiry to charity for a tax break. Spoilage is occurring at the client's own distribution centers, not at customer locations.
prompt.question: Despite the improvements already made, the client's spoilage rate of 7.5% remains significantly above the industry average of 2.5%. What can be done to further reduce the spoilage rate?

clarifying_info.a: Two channels: wholesale restaurant suppliers and supermarket chain bakeries.

clarifying_info.q: Where in the supply chain is spoilage occurring?
clarifying_info.a: Spoilage is occurring at the client's own distribution centers, not at customer locations.

clarifying_info.q: What is the shelf life of the product?
clarifying_info.a: Shelf life is 180 days; customers require at least 60 days remaining when they receive the product.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client's recipe compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Recipes are very similar across the industry and there are high switching costs to change recipes.

clarifying_info.q: Are the client's customers different from competitors' customers?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client serves the same customers as competitors.

clarifying_info.q: How many distribution centers does the client have?
clarifying_info.a: Three distribution centers: West, Midwest, and East — US sales only.

clarifying_info.q: What vendors does the client source materials from?
clarifying_info.a: Materials come from similar vendors as all other manufacturers. Materials themselves do not spoil; spoilage only occurs after the product has been manufactured.

framework: Investigate the full value chain for root causes of overproduction and spoilage: Demand Forecasting → Purchasing/Materials Sourcing → Manufacturing → Sales & Distribution → Customers
Demand Forecasting: assess accuracy and whether forecasting tools account for spoilage costs
Manufacturing: assess whether production volumes match forecasted demand or are systematically inflated
Sales & Distribution: assess SKU mix and customer-level volume patterns across the three DCs
Customers: assess whether all product types/SKUs have sufficient customer demand to justify production

questions.prompt: Walk through the value chain and identify where the root causes of excess spoilage likely lie.
questions.guidance: A strong answer maps the full supply chain from demand forecasting through to customers. The candidate should probe whether overproduction is demand-driven (bad forecasts) or supply-driven (production behavior), and whether the product mix includes low-velocity SKUs that contribute disproportionately to spoilage. Key findings to surface: (1) The forecasting tool is old and tends to generate overly cautious (high) production numbers, and does not fully account for spoilage costs; (2) The production foreman hedges against forecasts by deliberately overproducing because retooling the old machinery is time-consuming and painful; (3) Some products have very low customer turnover (low-volume SKUs), meaning certain dough varieties are rarely ordered and sit in DCs until they expire.

questions.prompt: What specific actions would you recommend to reduce spoilage?
questions.guidance: Candidate should map each root cause to an action: (1) Improve the forecasting tool to more accurately reflect actual demand and incorporate full spoilage cost in the model; (2) Long-term capital investment in updated manufacturing machinery with faster retooling times, removing the foreman's incentive to overproduce; (3) Conduct customer-level SKU rationalization — identify and eliminate low-volume SKUs where customer demand is too thin to justify production runs.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers exist across the value chain to further reduce spoilage from 7.5% toward the 2.5% competitor benchmark?

categories.name: Demand Forecasting
ideas: Upgrade the forecasting tool to use more granular historical demand data
Incorporate full spoilage cost into production planning models
Use rolling short-cycle forecasts rather than static long-horizon plans

categories.name: Manufacturing
ideas: Invest in modern equipment with faster retooling times to reduce overproduction incentive
Implement smaller, more frequent production runs aligned to actual demand
Align production foreman KPIs to spoilage rate, not just throughput

categories.name: SKU Rationalization
ideas: Conduct customer-level analysis to identify low-volume SKUs
Eliminate or consolidate SKUs with insufficient customer demand
Set minimum order volume thresholds for keeping a SKU in the portfolio

categories.name: Distribution & Inventory
ideas: Continue optimizing FIFO across all three DCs
Improve DC-level demand visibility to enable better inter-DC transfers
Reduce safety stock levels now that FIFO and donation programs are in place

recommendation: The primary drivers of excess spoilage are overproduction (caused by an outdated forecasting tool and a foreman who systematically overproduces to avoid retooling) and a long tail of low-volume SKUs that do not turn fast enough to avoid expiry.

To reach the 2.5% competitor benchmark, the client should: (1) upgrade the demand forecasting tool and build in full spoilage cost; (2) invest in modern manufacturing equipment with faster retooling to remove the overproduction incentive; and (3) rationalize the SKU portfolio by eliminating low-volume customer SKUs.
risks: SKU rationalization may create customer pushback or lost revenue if some customers value niche product types
Capital investment in new equipment requires upfront cost justification; payback period should be modeled against spoilage savings
Forecasting improvements take time to tune and may not immediately close the gap to 2.5%
next_steps: Quantify annual spoilage cost at 7.5% vs. 2.5% to size the financial opportunity
Model ROI of new manufacturing equipment against spoilage reduction benefit
Run customer-level SKU analysis to identify candidates for elimination with minimal revenue impact
Pilot improved forecasting tool at one DC before rolling out across all three
